items.key: ai:'12 weeks and so disgusted by my dog': what happens when you're pregnant and can't stand your pet?
items.text: ‘12 weeks and SO disgusted by my dog’: what happens when you’re pregnant and can’t stand your pet?
items.article: There may be almost no research on pet aversion during and post-pregnancy, but it may not be particularly rare About three weeks into her first pregnancy, Sylvia Luu began to loathe the smell of her border collie mix, Ranger. Luu could hardly be in the same room as Ranger without becoming nauseous. His drool repulsed her, and she found the smell of his fur so disgusting she wore a nose plug all day. “Before pregnancy, I used to smell my dog’s paws a lot,” says Luu. “But during pregnancy, I would throw up if I ever tried that.” At the time, Luu, 35, and Ranger had enjoyed 12 happy years together. Ranger slept in Luu’s bed. She walked him in all weather, and let him lick her face. Luu’s doctor said that her nausea was normal and simply advised her to drink more water to avoid dehydration from vomiting, but that didn’t alleviate Luu’s distress. “I was so heartbroken that I couldn’t love my dog as much as I wanted to,” says Luu, whose husband took over pet care duties. She wondered about rehoming Ranger, and was relieved when, upon delivering her firstborn, her aversion vanished. By the time of her second pregnancy, Luu was diagnosed with hyperemesis gravidarum . The condition is caused by hormonal shifts , much like the more familiar morning sickness. For 1%-3% of pregnant people, these shifts result in extreme nausea and disgust sensitivity that can be triggered by any number of things – in this case, pet odour.

items.article: Several prominent leaders, including Madan Malaviya, C Rajagopalachari and Rajendra Prasad, were involved in efforts to find a solution. IN THE autumn of 1932, Rabindranath Tagore boarded a train at Santiniketan for a long journey to Poona. Two months earlier, British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald had announced the Communal Award, which provided for separate electorates for various religious minorities and the Depressed Classes. Among its prominent supporters was BR Ambedkar, while Mahatma Gandhi, who was lodged at Yerawada Central Jail at the time, strongly opposed separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. “The British had originally decided to separate Hindus and Muslims into West Bengal and East Bengal. Ambedkar saw this as an opportunity to have a separate electorate for the depressed classes because upper-caste Hindus had never accepted them as Hindus. That’s the position Ambedkar took and Gandhi completely disagreed with that,” says Vijay Padaki, a theatre educator and playwright whose play The Prophet and The Poet examines the relationship between Gandhi and Tagore. Gandhi had declared that he would resist the proposal with his life. On September 20, he began a fast unto death. In one survey of people who take these medications, 20% of respondents experienced hair shedding, although the lack of high-quality data from a randomized, controlled trial to assess this side-effect makes it difficult to know exactly how common it is. While GLP-1-related hair loss is often temporary and reversible, it’s significant enough that some patients hesitate to take drugs they would otherwise benefit from using. What grows in a region, how much water is available, how humid the air is and how easily food can be preserved have all influenced what communities put on their plates. From desert berries to rainfed millets and foods preserved over smoky hearths, these dishes tell stories of adaptation. Bajra roti therefore represents more than a staple bread. It reflects a farming system built around crops capable of coping with water scarcity. items.text: Houseplant hacks: should you water plants less in winter?
items.article: Don’t water based on the month or the season – be led by what the plant is actually doing The problem Cutting back on watering for winter has become so ingrained that people start rationing by the calendar, giving plants just a fraction of the water they had in summer, because the season changed. The hack The advice to reduce is because, as light levels drop, most houseplants slow their growth, use less water and dry out more slowly, so watering as you did in summer risks waterlogging the roots and causing rot. The method When we get to October, reduce watering to half or a quarter of what you gave plants in the summer. The test I reduced watering in two of my own plants last winter. A calathea in a cooler, dimmer room dried out more slowly and needed less watering, exactly as the hack predicts. But a pothos sitting under a grow light in a warm room kept growing and started crisping at the edges and dropping yellow leaves. The verdict The winter watering rule is not a myth, but it is badly misunderstood. The key is to water according to what the plant is doing, not what the calendar says. Research your plant to see if it has a dormant season and check each plant before you water. Push a finger a couple of inches into the compost, or lift the pot to feel its weight – a bone-dry pot is light, a wet one is heavy.

items.article: Martin Ott said one of his biggest takeaways from working under Zuckerberg was learning how to use limited time effectively rather than trying to fill every available hour with work. Martin Ott, a former Meta executive who worked with Mark Zuckerberg during Facebook’s years of rapid expansion, says his time at the company taught him an important lesson about productivity: working longer does not necessarily mean getting more done. Ott, who is now the CEO of Berlin-based tax platform Taxfix, joined Facebook in 2012 as managing director for Northern and Central Europe. The company was still privately held at the time, shifting from desktop to mobile and had only a few thousand employees worldwide. Speaking to Fortune , Ott said one of his biggest takeaways from working under Zuckerberg was learning how to use limited time effectively rather than trying to fill every available hour with work. “There’s only so many hours in a day,” Ott said. Instead of trying to tackle everything, Ott believes leaders should identify the task that could have the greatest impact on a particular day. He also suggested being more selective about meetings and asking whether attending each one is actually necessary. “Ask yourself, what is the real one thing you could do today to really have impact, make a difference?” he said.

Sometimes it is deliberate. And sometimes the parents themselves are unaware of how often this happens. Parenting does not come with a handbook that tells two people how to agree on every decision. One parent may be stricter about screen time, while the other thinks an extra hour is harmless. One may believe that a teenager should be home by 7 pm, while the other says, “They are growing up, let them have some freedom.” One parent may insist that homework comes before play, while the other thinks the child has worked hard enough for the day. Differences are normal. In fact, they can be healthy. Children benefit from seeing that adults can think differently, negotiate, and still respect each other. The alleged attack by a co-pilot on the captain of a Flydubai flight has once again brought into focus one of aviation’s most difficult security questions: what happens when the threat comes not from a passenger trying to enter the cockpit, but from someone already inside it? The question has confronted aviation regulators before. Two deadly crashes , separated by more than 15 years, became central to the debate over the danger posed by a pilot left alone at the controls — EgyptAir Flight 990 in 1999 and Germanwings Flight 9525 in 2015. On October 31, 1999, EgyptAir Flight 990 took off from New York’s John F Kennedy International Airport for Cairo with 203 passengers and 14 crew members aboard. The Boeing 767 was cruising at about 33,000 feet when Captain Ahmed El-Habashi left the cockpit to go to the toilet. Relief first officer Gameel Al-Batouti was left at the controls. What happened over the next few minutes became the subject of a bitter dispute between American and Egyptian investigators. According to the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), Al-Batouti repeatedly said an Arabic phrase translated as “I rely on God".
